Dead Sea. The lowest point on Earth's surface at approximately fourteen hundred ten feet, or four hundred thirty meters, below sea level, straddling the border between Israel and Palestine-Jordan in the Levantine region. A hypersaline terminal lake fed by the Jordan River, it is so mineral-rich that the human body floats effortlessly, making it both geographically unique and historically symbolically charged. Its stark landscape of salt formations, mineral deposits, and barren shores has been inhabited and contested since antiquity, connecting biblical history, economic geology, and contemporary geopolitics.

At fourteen hundred ten feet below sea level, the Dead Sea is the lowest elevation on any terrestrial landmass and one of Earth's most extreme environments. The Jordan River feeds it from the north, but the Dead Sea has no outflow. This leads to evaporation and accumulation of dissolved minerals at roughly nine times the salinity of the Mediterranean.

Historical names include the Salt Sea from the Bible and the Sea of Lot from the Talmud, reflecting ancient Near Eastern geography and mythology. Mineral extraction has been conducted on industrial scales. Salt, potash, and bromine compounds are extracted commercially and form a major economic resource for surrounding regions. The sea's surface has dropped dramatically in recent decades due to reduced inflow from the Jordan River and intensive upstream irrigation, creating environmental concern.

Ancient Judean sites like Masada overlook its shores, making it a focal point in Jewish historical geography and memory. Its extreme salinity prevents most aquatic life, hence the biblical name. Only halophilic, salt-loving bacteria and algae survive, creating a unique ecosystem adapted to extremes.

Geologically, the Dead Sea occupies the southern portion of the Jordan Rift Valley, a tectonic depression marking the boundary between the Arabian and African plates. It is part of a vast geological fault system extending from Turkey to Mozambique. The mineral-rich waters and therapeutic mud have made it a destination for health tourism and dermatological treatment, adding economic value beyond industrial extraction. The Dead Sea connects to the Jordan River as the primary water source feeding it, to Israel which occupies the western shore and has invested in mineral extraction, to Palestine which shares the western shore and has historic claims, to Jordan which occupies the eastern shore, to the Negev Desert as the arid landscape surrounding its southern approaches, to the Middle East as the broader geopolitical region, and to Masada as the Judean fortress on its western shore, central to Jewish historical narrative.
